items.title: Air Purifiers as White Noise Machines
items.author: luu
items.content:
classic approach is a fan in a box, though in the past ten years people have mostly switched over to electronic ones. But a fan is really a great approach; you just need to put it to better use: have the fan clean the air.

Instead of spinning a fan in free air to make noise, you can have it pull air through a filter. A small purifier sounds a lot like a classic noise machine, is only a bit larger and more expensive, and removes smoke and infectious particles from the air. For example, here's a $47 purifier with a 6.5" diameter, cleaning 34 cubic feet of air per minute ("CADR") at 45dB. For most circumstances where someone would use a white noise machine, this kind of small purifier is all-around better.

Now, 34 CFM is not very much air cleaning. I usually run an AirFanta 3Pro and it cleans ~6x more air for the same amount of noise, or ~12x more air with much more noise (~56dB). On the other hand it's more expensive ($165) and bulkier (12.6" square), and arguably uglier.

Still, even a 34 CFM purifier helps a lot with smoke. If you have a 10ft square room with an 8ft ceiling and a reasonably typical 0.5 air changes per hour through leakage from outdoors, this small purifier will cut particulate levels to 16% of the outdoor level. In AQI terms (not linear) this is like going from AQI 200 to 72 or AQI 100 to 31.

items.title: Can we replace a $150k Looker with a bucket of HTML files?
items.author: skadamat
items.content:
Like a lot of companies, we pay for Looker. Let’s say $150k a year, the average Looker licence, roughly 300 seats. We are 3 data platform engineers at a company of about 500 people, and most of our week goes on the unglamorous stuff: keeping Snowflake fed, babysitting a dbt project that passed 2,000 models a while ago, and running the Airflow, Airbyte, DataHub and Kubernetes plumbing underneath it all.

In February, one of us built a thing on the side to host HTML files. It took an afternoon. 8 months later, and it’s already got as many weekly users as Looker in our company, maybe even more and Looker’s down a third.

SaaS is dead, apparently, so can we replace our enterprise BI tool?

Share of "self-hosted" GitHub repos

Meanwhile, "slop" on Hacker News

Left: share of new GitHub repos described as "self-hosted". Right: share of Hacker News comments saying "slop".

A year ago I thought most AI output was slop, and most of it was. We made a few “chat with your data” demos, and they looked great on a toy schema with 4 tables, but never really worked at our scale. The SQL ran without errors, but the numbers were wrong. That’s much worse.

Then Claude Code with Opus 4.5 got really good. Like, really good. In early January adoption across the company skyrocketed. It could work in our repos and use our tools. Also, it could run a query to check the numbers before answering. That mattered a lot more than getting a clever-sounding response. Within a few weeks, people in finance, ops and marketing who had never opened a terminal were prompting all day. All of a sudden everyone was prompting, and nobody was clicking.

Around this time, Claude started spitting out a lot of HTML. You would ask for an analysis and you’d get a single file with charts, and honestly, some of those pages looked better than our Looker dashboards. The problem was that it would live in someone’s Downloads folder. To share it, they would attach it in Slack and hope. This was way before Anthropic shipped shareable artifacts for Team and Enterprise (June 2026), and we really needed a way to share this new kind of dashboard.

We needed to host and share our HTML slop

One day Maddy from our team said she’d just put them all on a web server, with an internal domain name. By the end of the day she had vibe-coded the whole thing: a small service that stored the files in S3, SSO in front of it, and (some) tests. We already run everything on Kubernetes, so deploying a service was mostly a matter of adding a Terraform module and a Helm chart. Having all that plumbing in place made the whole thing much easier.

She wrote a small Python script and packaged it in a Claude plugin. Users would get their Claude to write the HTML, the script would push it (behind SSO), and anyone in the company could open the link. Initially, the files were just plain, static HTML. In March we thought, why not, and added a live query API using the viewer’s Snowflake OAuth token: best decision of the year.

Turns out, we didn’t need to write a permission model. Snowflake already had one all along. It had roles we’d been maintaining for years, and if Snowflake says you can’t read the sales table, then neither can the dashboard. By April, Snowflake OAuth was the only login.

People loved it, for a reason that's embarrassing for the BI industry: the dashboards actually looked good.

A Looker tile is a box with a fixed list of chart types and a fixed set of colours, and it looks like every other Looker tile ever made. Ugly, and no personality.

By getting rid of the rigid fixed tiles, our users could produce free-form HTML and prompt it until it looked neat. They loved it. Email and Slack exports came in April, parameters in May, and weekly viewers went from 23 in March to 136 in June. The exec team started to send links around. People also made the tool their own. They found use cases we would never have thought of, set dashboards to regenerate themselves on a schedule, added buttons, and built some wild designs and UX that no BI tool would have let them.

Security, at this point, was bad. Like, really bad. Dashboard JavaScript ran on the same origin as your session, nothing had permissions, and every employee could read every dashboard. It was basically one big XSS hole: any dashboard could run code as whoever opened it and pull data out in their name. We knew, and we shipped it anyway, because it was internal, behind VPN and SSO, and nothing else did this job.

In our team, “let’s just build a BI tool” became a running joke. It stayed a joke for a few months, until it became clear we were in too deep. We had piled months of vibe-coding onto something with a security model we weren’t proud of, and half the company was using it. We stopped joking and said it properly: let’s build a BI tool. We got in front of a whiteboard, mostly to work out how to fix the security model, and to agree on what we didn’t want to lose: the same S3 bucket, no migration, nothing breaking for the people already using it, and publishing that stayed as easy as before.

The one thing everyone agreed on: anyone can still push any HTML in one prompt, with no review step, no template and no list of approved widgets. We’d still defend that.

Every constraint you put between people and their dashboard sends them back to the Downloads folder.

The governance that matters already happens upstream, in dbt models and Snowflake roles. So the dashboard itself can stay as loose, as fast and as good-looking as people want.

There were 4 problems to solve.

One connector instead of a script. The upload script had been copied into 2 repos and a plugin, and every copy was a bit different. We replaced all of them with one remote MCP connector for the whole company, so claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude in Slack and our own analyst agent all call the same tools. The connector passes your Snowflake token along, and the API checks who you are with . Whatever an AI uploads lands as a draft, and a human has to click Publish.

Assume every dashboard is hostile. This is the part we needed to actually think about. The whole product is basically XSS by design: anyone can upload JavaScript that runs in a colleague’s browser, nobody reviews it, and the colleague might be the CFO. We can’t block the XSS, because the XSS is the product, so our job is to make sure it can’t reach anything. Our security model starts with “We assume it is hostile” for that reason. Each dashboard runs in a sandboxed iframe on its own origin, which gets no cookies and a strict CSP. The only thing it can talk to is the parent page, through , and the parent checks who sent the message, attaches the session and calls the API. Content tokens last an hour and work for one dashboard, one viewer and one host.

The sandbox protects the browser. We also created a separate metadata service that reads every new version of a dashboard async. It pulls out the whole HTML and the Snowflake queries. It checks for the scripts the page loads and where it sends data. Then a set of rules judges those facts. Most rules only report. They flag a dashboard that reads raw data instead of a dbt model, a script that isn’t pinned to a version, or a dashboard nobody has opened in 90 days. Some rules can block a dashboard: a script from a package nobody here has used before, or a WebRTC connection, which is the one way out that CSP can’t block. A blocked dashboard doesn’t load. The viewer sees a warning and has to accept it before the page runs.

Let Snowflake do identity and permissions. Every query runs with the viewer’s own token. Sharing a dashboard never shares data access. That’s a security feature, and it’s also a laziness feature: we never had to build or maintain data permissions, because everyone who logs in already has a Snowflake user with the right roles.

This part we vibe-coded in about a week, and it barely needed any design. For spaces, folders and sharing we copied Google Drive, because everybody already knows how Google Drive works: viewer, editor and owner, grants flow down the folder tree, and the strongest grant wins. Versions are stored by content hash, and restoring one gives you a draft. Then search, likes, scheduled exports, and teams synced from the HR system every hour. Compare that with the security model, which is where nearly all the real thinking went.

It took a few weeks of dev, and we got there.

Then it spread. People started tagging Claude in Slack threads and getting a dashboard back. Our analyst agent publishes its own, some repos publish straight from CI, and most people just publish from their own Claude, so every dashboard ends up looking a bit like the person who made it. These days it’s everywhere.

325 commits, about 74,000 lines of code (20,000 of them tests), and roughly $6.4k of Claude tokens.

That’s the whole bill on our side: 8 months, 3 engineers doing it on the side, plus a few friends who sent PRs. Claude wrote most of the code. We did the whiteboarding, argued a lot, and reviewed everything.

$0.50 a dashboard, what does that mean for BI?

People who used it, per week

Looker’s usage leaked rather than crashed. We haven’t moved everything: some teams still live in Looker, and some of its dashboards have no replacement yet. What made people use this instead of Looker is that building a dashboard stopped being expensive. That made us curious: how cheap, exactly? The good thing about paying in tokens instead of engineering time is that it’s easier to measure.

We use our analyst agent as a proxy here, because it’s a builder we can measure exactly. Every run is logged with its tokens and its cost, and every publish links back to the run that made it.

We found that each dashboard takes the agent around 1 million tokens, from the first question to the finished page. Now that we’ve moved it to Opus 5.5, the cost of a dashboard has dropped from about $2.50 to about $0.50. The agent does the same work; the tokens just got cheaper. That’s the real story: building software now costs whatever tokens cost, and that price keeps falling.

A BI tool is mostly a way to turn a query into a picture, and a picture now costs about $0.50 of tokens. It gets hard to justify a $150k licence for that part.

Here’s the bill for the whole thing, from the first commit in February to now.

8 months, February to October 2026
Built it ourselves
Looker licence8 months at the $150k average

Running it costs about $6k a year in AWS now that it has its own database, plus whatever Claude we spend to keep adding features, which has been around $1.3k a month since July. Call it $20k a year, against $150k for Looker, and most of that $20k is us building new stuff rather than keeping the lights on.

When we bought Looker we were buying 4 things: a UI to draw charts, a permission model, a semantic layer, and somewhere to host it. Claude now draws the charts, one dashboard at a time.

Snowflake had the permissions all along, dbt has the semantics, and hosting some HTML files costs about $500 a month.

Take those away and what’s left is a $150k invoice.

We’re not the only ones, either. You hear it more and more often: solid, established businesses cancelling very expensive analytics subscriptions. Amjad Masad told Platformer the same story about Replit: once he could join the warehouse to production Postgres and build the report himself, they “canceled or downsized most of [their] analytics products”.

In our case, building a dashboard tool around our existing stack has cost a fraction of what we were paying for Looker. For us, the important bits were already in dbt and Snowflake: the models, permissions and data. Looker sat on top of that and turned it into dashboards. That’s the part we’ve found we can replace.

The bill above also leaves out the biggest cost, which is us: 3 engineers spending 8 months on this, on top of everything else a data platform team does: the pipelines, the dbt project, the warehouse, the Kubernetes clusters, the on-call. None of that stopped. We can’t put an honest number on the hours, because they were spread across everything else we did. If you need to hire a team to build this, the maths is different.

If you already have a solid platform to build on and a team that knows it well, the rest is mostly Claude's time, and Claude's time is cheap.

I’d argue the line is scale. AWS and Snowflake sell things nobody can vibe-code: data centres, storage at petabyte prices, compute that’s cheap because millions of other customers share it. I think BI is particularly exposed because a lot of its value, at least for us, was in building and presenting dashboards. Claude can now do that for pennies. Products with a real scale advantage are a different story, but I wouldn’t be surprised if more companies start replacing parts of their BI stack themselves.

What about Claude Dashboards?

Anthropic announced Claude Dashboards in beta on 8 October, a week before this went up. So the obvious question: should we have just waited and bought that?

We couldn’t really. We started 8 months ago and it didn’t exist. If we were starting from scratch today, honestly, we’d probably look at it first. It’s AI-native, and it doesn’t have the rendering problems Looker has. If your team has nothing today, it’s probably the right call.

For us, the dashboards are only part of it. The tool is wired into the way our team already works: it talks to our agent control plane, our analytics platform and Slack, with a bunch of workflows we’ve built ourselves. Claude Dashboards might cover some of that, but we’d still have to work out how to connect it all. And if a feature changes or the price goes up, we’d have to deal with it.

So it’s still the same answer. If you need software that fits what you do, and you already have a platform to run it on and a dedicated team, build it, unless the moat is scale.

items.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and K3.1 Pro Highspeed
items.author: Jowsey
items.content:
We're introducing , the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities.

We are also releasing , which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.

Advancing the Frontier of Open Intelligence

Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains, we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.

Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On , which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%). And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon, our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores , above K3's .

K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools.

K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot, combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro:

K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of , an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller.

K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On , which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools, approaching the performance of and . From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections.

K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout.

Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences:

is now live on kimi.ai and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere.

With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis.

K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks:

  • evaluates formula linkage, financial logic, and final workbook quality in real-world modeling tasks. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 7.2 points.
  • evaluates whether models can produce auditable research under evidence and cutoff constraints. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 11.6 points.
  • evaluates long-horizon management and decision-making in a simulated business environment. K3.1 Pro achieves about 4.2× K3's performance.

Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.)

The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice:

As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness.

Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example.

After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits.

On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance.

These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure.

Kimi K3.1 Pro rolls out today across the Kimi product family: on Kimi.ai and the Kimi mobile apps, Kimi Work and Kimi Code, and through the Kimi API.

Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026.

  • Download the latest Kimi Work desktop app, version 3.1.0 or later, available for Windows and Apple silicon Macs.
  • Run Kimi Code and select Kimi K3.1 Pro using the command.
  • Visit the Kimi API Platform and select kimi-k3.1-pro / kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. Zero Data Retention is available for API customers.
  • Bring Kimi to your organization:Kimi Business provides enterprise-grade data privacy and member management, with complete separation between personal and organization accounts. Visit the pricing page and select “Get Kimi Business” to subscribe for your team.

Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results reported below are obtained with the reasoning effort set to 'max', temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95.

  1. Terminal-Bench Science 0.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. items.title: UUIDv7: Timestamps aren’t time-ordered and other oddities
items.author: ibobev
items.content:
Built on Shards of Silicon

I’m going to call it. UUIDv7 is weird.

Most blog posts about UUIDv7 tout these benefits:

  • monotonically increasing IDs
  • a helpful timestamp of when the object was created; and

But none of these properties are strictly held. Certain RFC compliant implementations of UUIDv7 violate these properties to extreme degrees. The only useful property UUIDv7 appears to strictly provide is uniqueness and therefore collision resistance. I’ve already discussed how UUIDv7 IDs can be guessable, so this post explores the other properties.

Superficially, it seems that embedding a timestamp in the ID can remove the need to track the creation time in a separate database column, providing marginally more efficient database operations. If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index.

Unfortunately, the timestamp embedded in a UUIDv7 ID may not relate to the object creation time. The Postgres docs for helpfully warn that “the extracted timestamp is not necessarily exactly equal to the time the UUID was generated”.

RFC 9562 allows implementations to alter the timestamp field, using values that aren’t strictly derived from the system clock. This relates to the tension between UUID monotonicity and timestamp accuracy. In certain scenarios, the difference between the timestamp and the current time can be arbitrarily large.

This specification makes no requirement or guarantee about how close the clock value needs to be to the actual time. — RFC 9562 §6.1

… implementations MAY increment the timestamp ahead of the actual time … — RFC 9562 §6.2

Incrementing the timestamp ahead of the system clock is an interesting problem. If the generator is seeing so much load that a counter field is regularly overflowing then the timestamp could accelerate into the future. Using a sufficiently large counter would be wise and the RFC says the minimum size SHOULD be 12 bits. A counter overflow would require a pretty aggressive creation rate, over 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node, which is beyond the limits of many systems. This overflow becomes relevant, however, if the timestamp freezes; which I’ll discuss in a later section.

Example: Python uuid.uuid7()

One prominent implementation that increments the timestamp is the Python standard library’s UUIDv7. The increment happens only in certain circumstances, like when the counter overflows. Unfortunately, the generator can get stuck in an increment cycle if the clock ever jumps backwards and the timestamp can race ahead of the system time by an arbitrarily large amount.

import uuid
from datetime import datetime

# Prime the generator with the current time
t = uuid.uuid7().time
now = datetime.now()
delta = (datetime.fromtimestamp(t/1000) - now).total_seconds()
print("Initial delta: ", delta)
# Ask the user to change the time
input("Set clock back one hour")

while True:
    for _ in range(100000):
        uuid.uuid7()
    t = uuid.uuid7().time
    now = datetime.now()
    delta = (datetime.fromtimestamp(t/1000) - now).total_seconds()
    print("New delta: ", delta)

$ uv run --python 3.14 main.py
Initial delta:  -0.000748
Set clock back one hour
New delta:  3695.277581
New delta:  3795.042411
New delta:  3894.80756
New delta:  3994.573106
^C

We expect the difference to be 3600 seconds (one hour) as the implementation refuses to allow the embedded timestamp to jump backwards and we expect the difference to decrease as the system clock catches up to the frozen timestamp. But when the load is above one ID per millisecond the difference will increase without bound. At lower loads it will take longer for the system clock to catch the timestamp, but we don’t see the runaway effect.

The related issue shows Python developers reasoning that this is consistent with the RFC, is consistent with other implementations, and that there isn’t “much we can do” on a “flawed system”. I think these points are correct as I see this same behavior in other implementations. Nevertheless, it would be helpful if existing UUIDv7 implementations could handle system clock jumps without runaway behavior. There are many real-world examples of clocks jumping backwards, even decades out of sync in time-sensitive environments.

Is leaking a timestamp harmful?

Embedding the timestamp in the ID means that you cannot share the ID without also sharing the timestamp.

It’s pretty difficult to think of an example where this really matters. One example could be a user profile page that doesn’t disclose when the account was created, but the UUIDv7 ID in the URL leaks the high-precision timestamp.

This issue would typically be very low on my list of security concerns because I find much more severe problems when I do security assessments. Nevertheless, there are contexts where this matters and engineering resources would be focused on addressing it. If you’re in the latter camp, be wary of UUIDv7 leaking metadata.

This section is even more pedantic, so skip ahead if you’ve had enough. Briefly: UUIDv7 IDs provide some sort of rough order, which may be suitable for your requirements.

When I was reading the UUIDv7 RFC I was surprised to see it describing a method for creating IDs across different nodes that are monotonically ordered. This was proven impossible back in the 1970s, and lead to the development of vector clocks and similar technology. At a high level, the problem is that system clocks cannot be synchronized to a suitable precision. Ordering things by timestamp only works if you know precisely what time it is. Any uncertainty in the time results in uncertainty of event ordering.

Succinctly: Timestamps are only time-ordered if you know what time it is and you don’t know what time it is.

For this reason, similar ID formats claim to be nearly sorted. It seems odd that UUIDv7 makes a stricter claim and does not deliver on them. At the very least, the challenges of synchronizing clocks across systems make the millisecond and especially the sub-millisecond timestamps quite suspect.

So no, there’s nothing in the UUIDv7 specification that would ensure the IDs are strictly monotonically increasing. Specific implementations may do better than others (with sub-millisecond timestamps, counters, well-synchronized clocks, etc), but we’ve known since the 1970s that this problem is not strictly solvable.

In UUIDv7’s favor, roughly ordered IDs are still quite useful. So don’t rip UUIDv7 out of your systems just yet. Just be wary of what assumptions you have.

Restarting a UUIDv7 generator

The RFC has lots of discussion about the handling of clocks that jump backwards. Timestamps are only time-ordered if clocks tick forwards, so special care is needed.

We’ve already discussed one mitigation: tracking the last generated timestamp to ensure that an earlier timestamp is never used. To do this safely you’ll need to write the last used timestamp to persistent storage, such that you can read it again after a system reboot or a process restart.

I’ve looked at several UUIDv7 implementations I couldn’t find one that writes timestamps to persistent storage. So implementers seems disinterested in addressing the issue and they generate out-of-order IDs when a process restart follows a clock jumping backwards.

Looking at real-world clock synchronization problems, you’ll find many examples of clocks getting set to future dates. When this happens, the backwards jump would align the timestamp to the actual time, but a last-used-timestamp guard would force timestamps to use keep using that incorrect timestamp until the system clock catches up. If the system clock takes a long time to catch up, you may start experiencing counter rollovers.

My mental model for UUIDv7 is that it’s a mash-up of a bunch of different ideas which implementations are free to choose as they see fit. There’s a wide variance of properties that UUIDv7 implementations can provide, with varying degrees of certainty they can successfully provide those properties. If you’re building your own implementation you can likely build something that has the properties you need. But most of us want to reach for an off-the-shelf version, especially when standard libraries provide an implementation, so we’re generally at the mercy of someone else’s implementation decisions. Implementations can change over time, making broad changes to their behavior while still being RFC compliant. Distributed systems may have multiple implementations across their subsystems, each with distinct properties. The only thing you can really expect is strong collision avoidance and ID uniqueness.

Be sure to ask these questions when picking a UUIDv7 implementation:

  • Is the implementation compliant with the RFC?
  • What additional properties does this implementation guarantee?
  • Under what limits can those guarantees be met?
  • Are there any assumptions required for these properties to hold, such as having an accurate system clock?
  • Under what conditions will the implementation alter the timestamp?
  • How guessable are the generated IDs?

Unfortunately, this sort of analysis is much more difficult than building an RFC compliant generator. Authors of UUIDv7 generators may not know the answers to these questions and may themselves be surprised that the RFC does handle this for them.

items.title: How is music possible
items.author: rafaelc
items.content:
Today, we listened to Swedish P2, where they were playing a mixtape that Sara Parkman had put together of folk music from around the world. I looked in the rearview mirror and saw that Maud, our nine-year-old, had closed her eyes. She does that when something is particularly good. It makes her see things, she says. Little films. Though she won’t say what they are. Parkman played a Sámi joik that had been recorded in Moscow a few months after the collapse of the Soviet Union,

and I turned off the main road, down one of the gravel paths through the beech forest, so I could slow the car to a walking pace and really listen. Rolling my window down and leaning out, I looked up at the slowly passing trees—they looked otherworldly wrapped in this music. I had never seen them like that before.

How can these landscapes arise?

approaching or leavinginfer the size and shape of a space from its echothe slightest pause or change in tonewe might speak with melodies that contain a lot of minor thirds

rate minor chords as positive

Now that I think about it, I suspect the reason I’m dissatisfied with all of the explanations of why music moves us comes down to this enormous distance between how simple the building blocks are and how far reaching their consequences.

I wonder if music is perhaps best thought of as an emergent phenomenon. It is built from small, mundane actions (plucking a string, manipulating our emotional processing, synchronizing our body movements with others to create a sense of bonding, and so on). But the thing that emerges (these swooping existential experiences) can’t be understood by just looking at the building blocks—much as the behavior of a sand dune can’t be understood by considering a single grain of sand. Sand dunes move around, larger ones more slowly than smaller ones, and when they collide, they exchange sand in various ways—none of which are properties that sand grains have.

However that may be, it is astounding that we get to live in a universe where music is possible. Absolutely astounding.

This essay benefitted from conversations with Andy Matuschak and Kristian Matsson. It was edited by Esha Rana.

items.title: Pentagon grants DHS permission to test heat ray weapon for use at border
items.author: bushwart
items.content:
The Pentagon has given the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a military-grade heat ray and develop tactics to potentially use it in operations at the southern US border, according to a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month and obtained by CNN.

The heat ray, officially known as the Active Denial System, is a nonlethal weapon that shoots an invisible beam of electromagnetic waves that can reach a little more than half a mile away, according to the US military.

The energy beam causes a burning sensation when it comes into contact with the human skin — which Pentagon officials have previously compared to feeling a blast of heat when opening a hot oven. Military officials have said the resulting “tingling effect” lasts between 10 and 15 minutes but also generates “an instinctive and irresistible urge to run from the effect.”

Deploying the heat ray at the US border would be an unprecedented step, even for the Trump administration, which has made border security and clamping down on immigration a top priority. The DHS request did not specify where or how the weapon would be tested and how it might eventually be used, but over the years, there have been internal discussions about potentially using it for crowd dispersal along the US-Mexico border, according to current and former Customs and Border Protection officials.

US officials had also considered deploying the system during moments of domestic unrest, including at the end of President Donald Trump’s first term when protests erupted over the murder of George Floyd, according to a former US official familiar with those discussions.

The memo authorizes the “temporary loan” of one ADS system for seven months, starting in September, and states that it “shall not be operated by DoW (Department of War) personnel,” appearing to absolve the Pentagon of any responsibility for how the directed-energy system may ultimately be deployed.

It also states that DHS is solely responsible for “system employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures.” At the end of the seven-month loan period, DHS can submit an additional request for further use of the Pentagon system in border operations based on need, a defense official told CNN.

“CBP is continually evaluating new technologies, especially those that enhance operational effectiveness and strengthen mission capabilities,” a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.

The Pentagon referred CNN to DHS when asked for comment.

The US military briefly deployed the system to Afghanistan nearly two decades ago but ultimately declined to use it during active combat operations. The US military also considered using the system for crowd control purposes at US facilities abroad where terrorist detainees were being held at the time but ultimately declined to employ it for that purpose as well, according to a source familiar with those previous internal considerations.

Customs and Border Protection officials have previously entertained the idea of using the system in areas where there’s a high concentration of illegal crossings. Border officials have occasionally discussed potentially using the system as a crowd dispersal tool, but it has never been deployed.

Officials ran into hurdles over legalities, use of force, effectiveness, and potential issues over sovereignty, particularly if the system was deployed on people in Mexico who had not yet crossed into the US. Chief among those concerns, however, was whether people could be harmed, either directly or indirectly, by the weapon.

“Even if they’re chasing people back to the river, you don’t want them to go in and drown,” a former CBP official told CNN. “For the cost, for the training and for the policies you’re going to create, is the juice worth the squeeze?”

El Centro sector, which covers around 70 miles along the US-Mexico border, evaluated the system several years ago, when Rodney Scott, who now serves as CBP commissioner, helmed that sector, according to a CBP official.

At the time, officials were discussing whether the system might help agents with an influx of illegal crossings along the nearby river by discouraging people from trying to cross in that area or pushing them to get out of the water.

One of the considerations at the time was whether the system might result in more rescues if people were incapacitated by the technology, the official said, though it’s unclear why it wasn’t deployed.

In 2018, prior to midterms, CBP officials also weighed using it against migrants, but then-Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen shot it down.

“The issue was treating immigrants and citizens like enemy combatants,” a former DHS official familiar with previous discussions about using the weapon against migrants told CNN. “Thematically, inhumane treatments typically get rejected.”

Some Border Patrol agents have more recently cast doubt over whether they need the tool at all amid low border crossings and an increase in personnel, according to another former CBP official.

gemma-4-26B-A4B is Google's sparse mixture of experts — 26B parameters with about 4B active per token. It is the third model family we have applied this work to, after Qwen and NVIDIA. On this one we put extra effort into keeping the accuracy intact: thinking comes down 38.9% on average at a cost of only 0.15pp of accuracy, which is smaller than the run-to-run spread on most of the suite.

Video comparison of the original model and the ThinkingCap model, prompted with the same input.Both models run on the same hardware and use the same inference settings.

We start with gemma-4-26B-A4B-it. The goal is to spend fewer tokens getting to the answer, and change nothing else: preserve the knowledge, reasoning ability, answer quality, instruction following and safety behaviour.

Mean thinking tokens per task family, gemma-4-26B-A4B-it against the ThinkingCap model

The thinking is where the change is, and every family gets shorter. Long-context and multimodal reduces the most, 54.4%, then knowledge and reasoning at 44.4%, maths at 36.1% and code at 27.6%; instruction following and agentic reduces the least at 17.2%. Averaged over the twelve benchmarks it is .

Long-context & multimodal
Instruction following & agentic

Every row is the original BF16 against the ThinkingCap model, run on the same harness with the same settings on the same questions. Accuracy is the mean over seeds, ± the 95% confidence interval from the spread between them. Every cell in the last row is an average across the twelve benchmarks, each counting once — so there is the mean of the twelve reductions, not the ratio of the two token figures beside it, which is 38.5%. The same distinction applies to the family bars above, which plot each family's mean tokens. On τ²-bench the thinking tokens are per task, summed across the rollout's turns, rather than per response. Every one of the twelve gets shorter. The deepest cuts are LongBench v2 (−69.1%), AA-LCR (−59.3%) and MMLU-Pro (−49.1%); the shallowest IFBench (−13.7%) and τ²-bench (−20.8%). items.author: eustoria
items.content:
A free and open source alternative Twitter front-end focused on privacy and performance. Inspired by the Invidious project.

  • All requests go through the backend, client never talks to Twitter
  • Prevents Twitter from tracking your IP or JavaScript fingerprint
  • Uses Twitter's unofficial API (no developer account required)
  • Lightweight (thanks to @nim_lang, 60KB vs 784KB from twitter.com)
  • Mobile support (responsive design)

This repository does not accept Pull Requests, but contributions are welcome in the form of , which can be submitted on an issue and are much more convenient to merge and work with.

It's impossible to use Twitter without JavaScript enabled, and as of 2024 you need to sign up. For privacy-minded folks, preventing JavaScript analytics and IP-based tracking is important, but apart from using a VPN and uBlock/uMatrix, it's impossible. Despite being behind a VPN and using heavy-duty adblockers, you can get accurately tracked with your browser's fingerprint, no JavaScript required. This all became particularly important after Twitter removed the ability for users to control whether their data gets sent to advertisers.

Using an instance of Nitter (hosted on a VPS for example), you can browse Twitter without JavaScript while retaining your privacy. In addition to respecting your privacy, Nitter is on average around 15 times lighter than Twitter, and in most cases serves pages faster (eg. timelines load 2-4x faster).

docker build -t nitter:latest .
docker run -v /nitter.conf:/src/nitter.conf -d --network host nitter:latest

A prebuilt Docker image is provided as well:

items.title: Is this the new cyber normal?
items.author: drewsberry
items.content:
The last week has seen a flurry of severe and critical software vulnerabilities affecting thousands of major sites and sending people into a panic. What’s going on here, and what can we do about it?

If we want to understand what’s going on in the world of software security at the moment, we need to understand what’s going on with all these bugs. I’m not a cybersecurity expert, so I’m going to link to external explanations instead of going into the gory technical details myself as these people are always going to do a better job at that.

Two different security teams, one from California security company Calif (as part of OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” program) and another from Israeli-U.S. cloud security company Wiz (they’re part of Google Cloud, apparently), both found these two Remote Code Execution (RCE) bugs in PHP. They were both using frontier AI models (a.k.a. LLMs, specifically GPT-5.6 Sol/Gemini 4 Argon) to find these vulnerabilities and build the exploits.

Interestingly, one of the bugs (CVE-2026-109618) was found by a security audit the PHP Foundation did in 2024 (funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency which is coincidentally one of the most interesting things happening in the open source space at the moment) but they basically ignored it because they had bigger concerns and couldn’t agree on a fix. The reasoning behind it was that no-one could really figure out how to create an actual exploit based on the theoretical issue.

One thing LLMs are very good at is taking a theoretical security vulnerability, even if that vulnerability is a vague description of what the issue could be, and building it into a full exploit. This has become a major issue in recent months as any notice of a security patch will immediately result in people pointing their LLMs at the codebase, whereupon the agents can very quickly read through diffs until they find something that looks like a security patch, then go backwards to the vulnerability it covers, and follow this all the way to an exploit.

This happens so fast, in fact, that at this point I think it is a reasonable that the moment you announce a security patch should be taken as a last possible date that the full exploit is being publicly or privately distributed.

Someone called petecooper posted on Hacker Newsabout the CVEs, apparently unaware that there even was an embargo. This (and other apparent leaks) prompted this hurried statement from the PHP Group and bringing the patch forward from Thursday 22nd to Wednesday 21st. However, the patch still wasn’t going to be available till the next day. This unintentional leak included CVSS scores of 10.0 (i.e. , although weirdly the actual scores were 9.2 instead).

Pretty much immediately, this news spread like wildfire and people started panicking. Even though this was found by “responsible security researchers” at , by the time the security patch actually got released, it was already being exploited in the wild. The PHP Foundation blamed Calif and a company called Chainguard by saying that Calif leaked a video of the exploit in action (with weird background music and a dancing anime girl) while Chainguard published fixes 6 hours before the embargo was due to lift, both allowing attackers to beat the systems administrators to the punch. The timeline is confusing, but it seems like multiple interconnected things have gone wrong here, all within the space of about 17 hours.

There’s been lots of discussion about whether AI really is the game changer that completely revolutionises computer security or not. The big AI companies (and they are big) obviously want you to think that it is. Some people argue that PHP2Shell is overblown because LLMs tend to be paranoid about vulnerabilities and come up with “exploits” that make bad assumptions (like that the server will run PHP code you upload yourself via some existing file inclusion vulnerability) or cheat in some way. As LiveOverflow points out, LLMs make it very easy to create exploit slop that proves nothing and doesn’t work, but that doesn’t mean that the vulnerability isn’t real and easy to exploit using AI. You can have 10,000 bad slop exploits that don’t work but if there’s one that does, that’s all that matters. Maybe we just need to get used to wading through slop to find the important stuff now.

Others point out that lots of governments (UK, EU, Japan, USA) got overexcited and released urgent announcements saying everyone had to unplug their computers immediately, so people panicked. I think the reason everyone panicked is that everyone kind of knows that PHP is intensely insecure and they use it anyway, so they’re kind of primed for bad news and to overreact. Also, it actually is really quite bad, so maybe panicking is kind of the correct reaction?

The big takeaway for me from this is that – because of LLMs – the time from “hey I heard there’s a bad RCE in this project” to “there are sophisticated, automated, and concerted attacks using an exploit targeting this vulnerability” has gone from weeks/months to hours/minutes. The fact that there’s loads of non-working exploit slop just shows how genuine expertise is still required to make these things – if you don’t know what you’re looking at, you can’t tell whether the AI has cheated or made bad assumptions.

On the exact same day (20th October 2026), Mozilla announced that they were blocking 8 intermediate certificates signed by Indian certificate authority eMudhra. This happened after a pseudonymous security researcher known only as “Wayne” reported to several big tech firms (such as Mozilla, Apple, Google, Microsoft, etc.) that the certificate authority were using laughably poor quality private keys for their intermediate certificates. Where a secure key might be a 100 digit number, eMudhra were using keys like “115”, “56”, and “4”. They must’ve been following RFC 1149.5:

There are no indications that this was found or exploited using AI or LLMs, although researcher Scott Helme notes that given a single prompt, Claude was able to recover the private keys of the intermediate certs.

At the time of writing (23rd Oct), eMudhra has announced that it will be retiring from the certificate authority space. In unrelated news, a farmer has announced that he has shut his stable door, following reports of an escaped horse.

The next day, cloud provider Railway announced that they found evidence that hackers had accessed and even decrypted environment variables from their platform, which often hold secrets such as database credentials, API keys, etc. In their statement, they said that they believed that this was part of a concerted effort aimed at compromising companies that provide AI inference.

What would the end goal be here? At the time of writing (23rd Oct), we have very little information to go on. Is this “unauthorized third party” (official announcements of “some randos got into our computers” always find a way to make it seem like a terms of service agreement, maybe that way they think people won’t pay attention to it) trying to spy on people using AI inference to see what they’re doing, even stealing new models or research? Or maybe they’re trying to build a network of compromised inference providers for their own nefarious generative AI purposes (like finding more PHP bugs).

On 12th October 2026, GitLab warned of a max severity bug in GitLab CI/CD’s regular expression parsing that could enable attackers to execute arbitrary code (another RCE) using a specially crafted regex. This is a CVSS score of 10.0 which is the maximum possible, meaning “this is pretty much as bad as they come”. This was followed on 21st October 2026 by yet another regex integer overflow RCE, another 10.0.

This follows hot on the heels of yet another 10.0 CVSS CVE from last month (CVE-2026-85706), that time related to path traversal. All three of these bugs were reported through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program. When it became clear that LLMs could research vulnerabilities and write exploits, there was a lot of talk about shutting down bug bounty programs because they didn’t make sense anymore. I’m sure GitLab are glad they didn’t do that now.

Although GitLab is used very widely across academia, government, and private companies, this doesn’t seem to have got as much attention. CVEs in GitLab are obviously very serious, especially for private companies, as a lot of their vitally important intellectual property is stored in there, and having that leak could be disastrous. Often, companies put their GitLab instance behind a VPN/firewall so that they aren’t publicly accessible, which greatly reduces the risk associated with this. It’s also not entirely clear whether these CVEs require specific conditions like publicly accessible projects, user self-registration, etc. It does seem like CVE-2026-110264 requires at least one public project, but I can’t find any information on the conditions around the earlier CVE.

There’s no indication that these were discovered using AI or LLMs. They may have been, but there’s no reason at this point to think they were.

On 21st October, a bug in musl’s libc related to regex (libc has regex? Apparently…) was announced that leads to denial of service at least, if not code execution. As far as I can tell, this is entirely coincidental in timing and not related to the GitLab bugs, which both also seem to be integer overflows when parsing untrusted regular expressions, one reported on the exact same day. Who knew a regex engine was such a security issue – is regex the new font rendering? The GitLab bugs were both found by a Swede called Johan Carlsson (joaxcar) while the musl bug was reported by Julien Voisin, a French self-proclaimed “open sourcerer”.

Ah, hello my old friend LiteLLM. Proving that, when you’re made of metal and 200 feet tall, lightning can in fact strike twice. It’s not a good sign that when someone asks whether you’ve heard of the big 2026 LiteLLM compromise, you have to ask “which one?” In a piece of good fortune, the whole PHP2Shell and all the others have cannibalised much of the attention, meaning this isn’t getting quite the same traction as last time in March, despite being similarly bad.

This time, it’s a malicious version on the Python Package Index (PyPI) and Docker images. For those who don’t remember, LiteLLM had a very similar thing happen back in March, where a malicious package was uploaded to the litellm package on PyPI that used the files to autoload malicious code (yeah, it was bad).

This compromise again took advantage of files and this time also the file for autoloading malicious payloads, running in the preload step as soon as the Python interpreter starts up. According to the analysis from Wiz, the payload has “strong indications of LLM-aided development” – things like overly verbose variable names, overly defensive error handling, brittle edge cases, and all the comments saying “this is where it really bites”, “it’s worth sitting with that”, “lean into that”, and “that stays yours” repeatedly.

According to LiteLLM, the incident occurred because the attacker had access to credentials for GitHub CLI which allowed them to run CI jobs. LiteLLM note that Claude Code will apparently sometimes embed a user’s GitHub CLI OAuth token into response bodies which could cause them to appear in LiteLLM logs.

On October 19th 2026, an enterprise software company called “PingCAP” that develops a database called “TiDB” revealed “unauthorised access to PingCAP” with “no evidence that data stored in TiDB was impacted”. At the same time, a cyber extortion group called “FulcrumSec” (a.k.a. the “Threatspians”) said they had exfiltrated 10.6 TB of data from PingCAP and publicly released a torrent with 200 GB of data, as a “stage one release” (you’ve gotta get people invested in the sequel).

They also posted full details of what they took and some of the excellent security practices of PingCAP, including putting client AWS secret access keys inside Jira tickets and attaching massive unredacted logs to Jira tickets including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, xAI API keys. Yikes. If you’re willing to visit the cyber extortion group’s website, they do a pretty interesting write-up of it. Gone are the days of shoddy broken English back when the Russians had to write these things up without LLMs to do it for them and remind them of definite and indefinite articles.

The good news for PingCAP is that not finding evidence of data extraction is actually incredibly easy. In fact, I’m doing it for thousands of companies right now, for free. I’m sure there’s a business proposal in there somewhere. All you have to do is not look (see also: U+1F648). To be fair, I think their argument is that no data was compromised. 10.6 TB seems like a lot of data if that’s the case. There’s clearly still tons of customer data.

Linux vulnerabilities accidentally posted in wrong group chat

Linux kernel development all happens through mailing lists. Naturally, some of those are about security sensitive things, so these are private. Over the night of 21st-22nd October 2026, the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), a software vulnerability initiative owned by Trend Micro, reported a bunch of high severity (upwards of 9.0 CVSS) CVEs to the public mailing list, instead of the private one. Naturally, the assumption is that anyone with an LLM and a heart full of dreams will then be able to take those reports and turn them into active exploits within a matter of minutes. This isn’t quite as bad as that time Pete Hegseth accidentally texted details of upcoming military strikes in Yemen to The Atlantic, but it’s still interesting how seriously people take this now.

I think it’s fair to say these last few days have been abnormally active in terms of all of these cyber incidents and security disclosures. There are many commenters on the Hacker News discussions for these incidents that say that this is nothing and it’s only going to get worse. Honestly, I’ve not decided yet. To be honest, if you’d asked me 4 years ago how far LLMs would go, I’d never have guessed they’d get as good as they are right now. Even so, people do tend to get overexcited by these announcements and suggest that we are going to live in a world where no software is secure and everyone is vulnerable.

It’s worth noting that while a lot of the online discussion around this focusses on AI and LLMs, only some of these disclosures were researched or created with LLMs. We don’t know about some of them like the PingCAP one, but there’s clear evidence that many criminal and state-sponsored groups are using AI to do more hacking and faster. Why wouldn’t they? It seems to be pretty good at it. Many of these vulnerabilities were good old fashioned software vulnerabilities found and written using human meat fingers, but the online conversation focusses on the exciting, scary new thing. Why wouldn’t it?

You can see why organisations like NHS England decided to take all of their open source code private (even though that was a silly decision). When these LLMs are so good that anyone can point their agent at some open source code and find tons of vulnerabilities, then write full exploits for them, that is concerning for many. So what’s the solution here?

  • Your code isn’t online anymore, so people can’t point their LLMs at it and do things like analyse every commit for security fixes, find tons of previously unknown critical bugs, etc.
  • The open source community and the future of computing are slightly worse off for every open source repository taken offline.
  • You can’t close source every codebase in the world – some things like programming languages (which are often the source of critical bugs) rely on open source to function. Making Python a closed source project would be catastrophic to the world of computing.
  • It’s only closed source until someone leaks it. And they probably will eventually. And when they do, you won’t have had the years of public scrutiny on the codebase that keeps it clean and secure in the first place.
  • Sometimes you use a programming language where this doesn’t really matter, like Python and Java where you can recover source code from bytecode.
  • LLMs can even reverse engineer compiled binaries pretty effectively.
  • If the code used to be online, that old version still is. You have to assume that someone will have it somewhere. Shellshock was in GNU Bash from 1989 until 2014 before it was fixed, and that’s one of the most widely used programs on the planet.

The AI-embracer approach: if you can’t beat ‘em, join ‘em. In other words, they can’t use LLMs to find vulnerabilities if we’ve already run our better LLMs on our code faster and with more money and better models.

  • Makes a few very wealthy tech CEOs very happy.
  • Makes a few very wealthy tech CEOs very happy.
  • Will find tons of bugs. (Someone is gonna have to fix those.)
  • Even though AI makes it easier, it still requires expertise and deep technical knowledge to do this stuff properly (for now).

The optimist approach: universally better, standardised approaches to reporting, handling, and mitigating security vulnerabilities followed by all companies having top-notch security postures, well-understood risks, well-documented processes, and so on.

  • Why didn’t anyone else think of this?
  • Gee, we are so clever. Have we just solved this?
  • We do not live in this world. We will never live in this world.
  • Did I mention this is actually quite hard? And possibly impossible?

There are some easy wins we could get from this moving forwards, like “never announce details of a critical vulnerability before the patch is ready to install”, but in this case unintentional leaks meant everyone knew about the vulnerabilities even before the official announcement. Maybe even that’s asking too much. In this case, it was a series of mistakes from multiple people and companies that led to or accelerated the exploit being in active use hours before the patch was available, hence everyone taking their servers offline. AWS have since said they saw someone trying out this vulnerability from 17th October, before any of these leaks happened.

Even something like minimum release age which gained popularity after shalk/debug, Shai-Hulud, & March LiteLLM incidents, as it means big updates that fix widely exploited vulnerabilities don’t get patched for a few days, giving attackers ample time to hack you to pieces. At the very least, we could maybe do with some better client management to avoid everyone panicking and taking all their servers offline.

Maybe we just need to accept that if you expose something to the wider internet, it will get hacked, and plan accordingly. Maybe it’s our expectations that are at fault.

There’s definitely a story about AI and security here. It’s changing the world of software, and it’s not yet clear whether that’s for the better or the worse. Money has a way of warping truth like matter warps spacetime, and there’s enough money in AI to cause whatever the truth equivalent of a medium-sized black hole is. There’s an incredible amount of money being spent on AI and it all wants you to think that it’s going to change everything about your life, including software and security. That doesn’t mean it’s not true, of course.

Some people say automated analysis tools led to loads of new bugs being found back in the ’10s, and now the same thing is happening again. It feels categorically different to me, but perhaps there will be an initial period of escalating bug reports before it all settles down and goes back to how it was. I suspect not. Some people say this is only happening because humans wrote all the dodgy code in the first place – once AI is writing all of the code to start with, there’ll be no vulnerabilities because LLMs are better at writing secure code than humans. I am not convinced by this argument.

While I’m not making many predictions about the future (because I don’t want to look like an idiot in 12 months’ time when I’m inevitably proven wrong), I will say that the software industry is going to change, and open source is going to change, and it is our collective responsibility as members of the software community to make sure that this change is for the benefit of all of us, not special interests and private corporations.

This is a developing story – I’ll note any updates in here. I wrote this in somewhat of a hurry, so I may also make some incremental improvements to the wording and evidencing behind some bits.

items.title: Job loss and cortisone mania
items.author: speckx
items.content:
On the morning of 18th August, I got invited at short notice into a 1:1 meeting by my manager, which was . I think I knew what was coming, and I was right: The company is restructuring, and I’m being let go (among a lot of other people). I had time until lunch to say my goodbyes to my colleagues as I would be logged out of my account after that. Because I was still in my six-month probation period, I was put on paid leave for two more weeks; after that I’d be out of a job for the first time since I started working roughly 10 years ago.

I’ve seen it happen to other people and entire departments, but it had never happened to me — I guess I’m a real tech worker now!

Shortly after, I got sick. I believe it was a Covid infection; I didn’t have any respiratory symptoms, but low energy, joint pain and general feelings of stiffness. Every move was a show of strength. I developed a cough that is now — 2 months later — still subsiding but present.

I’m not sure if it was Covid, but being sick triggered the autoimmune condition I have. I mostly got out of bed, watched shorts, videos and movies, and then I went to bed again. I had to take some trips into the city by bike, and hours later it would hit me like a brick wall, leaving me even more exhausted on the next day. I lost my appetite and some weight, which is not good since I rarely moved and I’m fairly lean to begin with.

This state dragged on for three weeks until I went to see a specialist and got all the blood work and tests done, so that my medication could get adjusted. Being sick for a couple of days is something I can bear, but not being able to perform even the smallest tasks for such a long time was a disheartening experience.

I was put on cortisone treatment, which relieved my symptoms immediately. Cortisone essentially lowers your body’s immune response — which is great when your body tries to defend itself against itself, like mine did. On the other hand, cortisone is not meant for long-term or permanent treatment, and it has a lot of potential side effects.

After one or two days, I was back to my normal self, energised, vital, with no signs of inflammation. I now fully realised that I was out of a job, and had the chance to fill my time meaningfully. Job searching doesn’t take up your 16 waking hours.

In some phases of my life, I can take a giant step back, and look at it like from a bird’s eye view. I’m approaching 30, but how will I live when I’m 40, 50, 60, 70 years of age? Will I be healthy? Will I still pursue my hobbies? Will I have children, or grandchildren even? Who will be close to me? I can’t force my fate, but I can make conscious decisions every day to aid this transition. I felt mindful, present in the moment, and free. Lucid.

So I researched a sleep routine. Cleaned the entire apartment. Discarded useless stuff. Created lists and overviews. Organised. Shopping lists. Meal plans. Jotted down recipes. Fixed broken things. Impulse-bought some personal items for my living room.

I addressed tiny things that stuck out to me more than once, like a mark on the wall that I painted over, or re-seasoning my cast-iron pan since it was in a bad state. Every time I looked at these, I felt remorse or the need to do them, but never followed through.

I did all of this, and it felt incredible. Focusing on something, and realising it (as in putting it into reality). Self-efficacy. While I can’t vouch for the movie, it surely felt like this scene from Limitless.

I didn’t realise right away, but I was feeling strong signs of restlessness. My heart felt like it was racing, even though I wasn’t doing anything exhausting. I couldn’t sit still for an extended time. My mind was jumping from thought to thought. I felt like a wound-up toy, manic. I used this frenzy to tackle all the chores and tasks and projects and minuscule things, and yet I still kind of liked it. 110% productivity.

Other side effects I noticed: My face swelled up a bit, making it look more full (which looks good on me tho). My knee joints feel weird. My sleep is basically broken: I go to bed at 23:00–00:00 every day, and try to wake up at 8:00. The routine is there, but falling asleep actually takes some time, and I usually wake up at 5:00 or 6:00, completely awake. Not necessarily fully rested, but not sleepy anymore.

Right now, I feel healthy and great. As I’m tapering off the cortisone, the side effects will cease, but all the work I put into improving my daily life will still be there.

Maybe this post can inspire you to take a step back from your own life, and assess your priorities. I can rarely get into this mindset, but when I do, it makes me feel serene, in control. Every day life can get to you in so many ways.

items.title: The foolishness of "natural language programming" (1978)
items.author: xiaoyu2006
items.content:
On the foolishness of "natural language programming".

Since the early days of automatic computing we have had people that have felt it as a shortcoming that programming required the care and accuracy that is characteristic for the use of any formal symbolism. They blamed the mechanical slave for its strict obedience with which it carried out its given instructions, even if a moment's thought would have revealed that those instructions contained an obvious mistake. "But a moment is a long time, and thought is a painful process." (A.E.Housman). They eagerly hoped and waited for more sensible machinery that would refuse to embark on such nonsensical activities as a trivial clerical error evoked at the time.

Machine code, with its absence of almost any form of redundancy, was soon identified as a needlessly risky interface between man and machine. Partly in response to this recognition so-called "high-level programming languages" were developed, and, as time went by, we learned to a certain extent how to enhance the protection against silly mistakes. It was a significant improvement that now many a silly mistake did result in an error message instead of in an erroneous answer. (And even this improvement wasn't universally appreciated: some people found error messages they couldn't ignore more annoying than wrong results, and, when judging the relative merits of programming languages, some still seem to equate "the ease of programming" with the ease of making undetected mistakes.) The (abstract) machine corresponding to a programming language remained, however, a faithful slave, i.e. the nonsensible automaton perfectly capable of carrying out nonsensical instructions. Programming remained the use of a formal symbolism and, as such, continued to require the care and accuracy required before.

In order to make machines significantly easier to use, it has been proposed (to try) to design machines that we could instruct in our native tongues. this would, admittedly, make the machines much more complicated, but, it was argued, by letting the machine carry a larger share of the burden, life would become easier for us. It sounds sensible provided you blame the obligation to use a formal symbolism as the source of your difficulties. But is the argument valid? I doubt.

We know in the meantime that the choice of an interface is not just a division of (a fixed amount of) labour, because the work involved in co-operating and communicating across the interface has to be added. We know in the meantime —from sobering experience, I may add— that a change of interface can easily increase at both sides of the fence the amount of work to be done (even drastically so). Hence the increased preference for what are now called "narrow interfaces". Therefore, although changing to communication between machine and man conducted in the latter's native tongue would greatly increase the machine's burden, we have to challenge the assumption that this would simplify man's life.

A short look at the history of mathematics shows how justified this challenge is. Greek mathematics got stuck because it remained a verbal, pictorial activity, Moslem "algebra", after a timid attempt at symbolism, died when it returned to the rhetoric style, and the modern civilized world could only emerge —for better or for worse— when Western Europe could free itself from the fetters of medieval scholasticism —a vain attempt at verbal precision!— thanks to the carefully, or at least consciously designed formal symbolisms that we owe to people like Vieta, Descartes, Leibniz, and (later) Boole.

The virtue of formal texts is that their manipulations, in order to be legitimate, need to satisfy only a few simple rules; they are, when you come to think of it, an amazingly effective tool for ruling out all sorts of nonsense that, when we use our native tongues, are almost impossible to avoid.

Instead of regarding the obligation to use formal symbols as a burden, we should regard the convenience of using them as a privilege: thanks to them, school children can learn to do what in earlier days only genius could achieve. (This was evidently not understood by the author that wrote —in 1977— in the preface of a technical report that "even the standard symbols used for logical connectives have been avoided for the sake of clarity". The occurrence of that sentence suggests that the author's misunderstanding is not confined to him alone.) When all is said and told, the "naturalness" with which we use our native tongues boils down to the ease with which we can use them for making statements the nonsense of which is not obvious.

It may be illuminating to try to imagine what would have happened if, right from the start our native tongue would have been the only vehicle for the input into and the output from our information processing equipment. My considered guess is that history would, in a sense, have repeated itself, and that computer science would consist mainly of the indeed black art how to bootstrap from there to a sufficiently well-defined formal system. We would need all the intellect in the world to get the interface narrow enough to be usable, and, in view of the history of mankind, it may not be overly pessimistic to guess that to do the job well enough would require again a few thousand years.

. As a result of the educational trend away from intellectual discipline, the last decades have shown in the Western world a sharp decline of people's mastery of their own language: many people that by the standards of a previous generation should know better, are no longer able to use their native tongue effectively, even for purposes for which it is pretty adequate. (You have only to look at the indeed alarming amount of on close reading meaningless verbiage in scientific articles, technical reports, government publications etc.) This phenomenon —known as "The New Illiteracy"— should discourage those believers in natural language programming that lack the technical insight needed to predict its failure. (End of remark.)

From one gut feeling I derive much consolation: I suspect that machines to be programmed in our native tongues —be it Dutch, English, American, French, German, or Swahili— are as damned difficult to make as they would be to use.

items.title: Jank – The native Clojure dialect with seamless C++ interop
items.author: giancarlostoro
items.content:
The native Clojure dialect with seamless C++ interop

jank is Clojure on top of C++. It has C++ interop unlike any other language. Templates, virtual functions, exceptions, overload resolution, and RAII all just work in jank. No boilerplate necessary. Just include your headers and go!

jank is a robust Clojure dialect. It offers interactive REPL-driven development powered by a Clang-based C++ JIT compiler.
